Senses.Explanation: This paired verdict catches one move falling short and another overshooting. Fushan Fayuan applies it to Yongjia’s encounter with Huineng, and later speakers turn it into a public question about how to be exactly right. The two halves are inseparable: the first judges an earlier action as not reaching, while the second judges the later action as excessive. Tian’an Sheng asks his assembly how one can “get it exactly right” between them; Yezhu Fuhui asks who the person described by both clauses is.

Senses.Note: Mere explanation outside this teacher-student presentation is excluded.

Senses.Explanation: The numinous or divining tortoise appears with shell, omens, diagram, book, and a tail that leaves traces. The most frequent Chan family is “the numinous tortoise drags its tail” (靈龜曳尾). The corpus explains the material action: on the ground it wipes its track, but the track arises again (拂迹迹生, “it brushes away the trace and the trace appears”). The Blue Cliff Record says that even someone with flashing responsiveness cannot avoid the tortoise dragging its tail. A later comment applies the same action to the Buddha holding up the flower and says traces are hard to remove. Asked for the Five Ranks, Boshan Suru Han answers that the numinous tortoise has no omen-lines and its empty shell need not be drilled. Other addresses have the tortoise enter the sea and swallow the moon, or pair the river-horse carrying a diagram with the tortoise bearing a book. The Zen-specific bend is the repeated use of this divining animal's tail, track, shell, omen, diagram, and burden as public comment, answer, and teaching-seat image; the entry does not convert those actions into a single abstract lesson.

Senses.Explanation: The numinous turtle drags its tail and thereby leaves the trace that betrays it. Chan masters use the image when an apparently quick, subtle, or traceless performance still exposes a residual mark by which it can be caught. Yuanwu says even lightning-fast eyes and function do not escape it; Tianran applies it to assertions of either mind and Way or no mind and no Way; Jianmen Nan says even perfect handling of the three seals leaves the tail; and Mingjue Cong calls an entry-answer the turtle’s self-made omen of ruin. Yuanwu also applies it to Xuedou’s added comment, and Dawei Jinglun uses it for Wuzu Fayan’s saying that cannot be retracted once heard.
